title: Can You Do a 1031 Exchange on a Flip Property? What Investors Need to Know
excerpt: Many real estate investors wonder if they can use a 1031 exchange to defer taxes on a flip property. The short answer is complicated — and understanding the rules could save you tens of thousands of dollars.
author: AIWholesail Team
metaDescription: Can you do a 1031 exchange on a flip property? Learn the IRS rules, key exceptions, and smart tax strategies for real estate investors in 2024.

sections.content: You just sold a flip for a $60,000 profit. Now the IRS wants a big chunk of it. Naturally, you start wondering: can you do a 1031 exchange on a flip property and kick that tax bill down the road? It's one of the most common questions in real estate investing — and the answer depends on a few critical details most investors overlook.
The Short Answer: Usually No — But There Are Exceptions

In most cases, the IRS will not allow you to use a 1031 exchange on a property you flipped. The reason comes down to one key phrase in the tax code: 'held for investment or productive use in a trade or business.' A traditional flip — where you buy a distressed home, renovate it, and sell it within a few months — does not meet this standard. The IRS considers those profits ordinary income, not capital gains, and 1031 exchanges are specifically designed for capital gains deferral.

'The 1031 exchange is one of the most powerful wealth-building tools in real estate — but it was built for investors, not dealers. Knowing the difference between the two can mean the difference between a massive tax bill and none at all.' — Tax attorney specializing in real estate
Why the IRS Treats Flippers Differently

The IRS uses the term 'dealer' to describe investors who buy and sell properties regularly as a business activity — essentially, anyone treating real estate like inventory. If you are a dealer, your profits are taxed as ordinary income, which can reach up to 37% federally, plus self-employment tax in some cases. Investors who hold property for appreciation or rental income are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rate of 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on their income bracket. Only that second group — investors — can typically take advantage of a 1031 exchange.
What Makes Someone a 'Dealer' vs. an 'Investor'?

There is no single bright-line rule, but the IRS looks at several factors to determine your status. If you are flipping multiple properties per year, advertising them for sale, and treating the activity as your primary business, you are almost certainly a dealer. This is important context — even if you have held a property for more than a year, the IRS may still deny your 1031 exchange if the facts suggest you intended to flip it from day one.

items: How long you held the property before selling
Whether you actively marketed the property for sale
How many properties you have bought and sold in recent years
Whether you have a business entity set up for flipping
Your stated intent at the time of purchase
Whether you made significant improvements to resell, not to hold

sections.content: The Exception: When a 1031 Exchange on a Flip Might Work

Here is where it gets interesting. If you can demonstrate that you originally purchased the property with the intent to hold it as a rental or long-term investment — and then your plans changed — you may have a stronger case for a 1031 exchange. The key is documented intent. For example, if you purchased a duplex, rented it out for at least 12 to 24 months, and then decided to sell, you have a much better argument that it was held for investment purposes. Some tax professionals recommend a minimum holding period of two years to strengthen that case, though there is no guarantee.

Pro Tip: Before purchasing any property, document your intent in writing. If you plan to hold it as a rental, put that in your business plan, LLC operating agreement, or even a simple dated memo. This paper trail can be invaluable if the IRS ever questions your 1031 eligibility.
The 'Flip-to-Rent' Strategy: A Legitimate Path to a 1031

One strategy gaining popularity among savvy investors is to rehab a property, rent it out for a period of time, and then sell it via a 1031 exchange into a larger investment property. This approach lets you capture the forced appreciation from the renovation while also qualifying for the tax deferral. The rental income during the hold period is a bonus, and the 1031 allows you to roll gains into your next deal without a tax haircut.
Step-by-Step: How to Structure a Flip for Potential 1031 Eligibility
If you want to keep your 1031 options open, you need to be intentional from the very beginning of your deal. Here is a practical framework for structuring your next project with tax strategy in mind.

items: Step 1 — Document intent at acquisition: Write a brief memo stating you intend to hold the property as a rental investment after renovations are complete.

Step 2 — Estimate your rehab costs accurately: Use the free [Rehab Estimator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator) to project costs before you buy, so you know your numbers going in.
Step 3 — Complete the renovation and place the property in service as a rental: Find a tenant and begin collecting rent. Ideally, hold for at least 12 to 24 months.
Step 4 — Consult a qualified intermediary (QI): A QI is required to facilitate a 1031 exchange. Find one before you list the property for sale.
Step 5 — Identify your replacement property within 45 days: This is a hard IRS deadline. Have a target property in mind before you close on the sale.
Step 6 — Close on the replacement property within 180 days: The entire exchange must be completed within this window, no exceptions.
Step 7 — Work with a real estate CPA: Have a tax professional review your full situation before proceeding. Everyone's facts are different.

sections.content: What Happens If You Try to 1031 a True Flip?

If the IRS determines that your property was dealer inventory rather than an investment, the exchange will be disallowed. That means you will owe ordinary income tax on the full profit — potentially 37% or more when you factor in state taxes and self-employment tax. The IRS may also assess penalties and interest if you tried to defer taxes you were not legally entitled to defer. It is simply not worth the risk without a solid legal foundation. Wholesalers: A Special Note

If you are wholesaling real estate, the news is even more clear-cut: wholesale assignment fees are not eligible for 1031 exchange treatment. Wholesale profits are ordinary income, full stop. That does not mean wholesaling is a bad strategy — it can be an excellent way to build capital with low risk — but tax deferral is not part of the equation. If you are just getting started, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) can help you understand the business model and where your profits actually come from.

Pro Tip: Some investors run two separate business entities — one LLC for flipping (dealer activity) and a separate entity for long-term investment properties. This separation can help protect your investment properties' 1031 eligibility from being tainted by your flip activity. Always consult a CPA or tax attorney before setting this up.
The Bottom Line on 1031 Exchanges and Flips

Can you do a 1031 exchange on a flip property? In most traditional flip scenarios, no. But with careful planning, proper documentation, and the right holding strategy, you can absolutely structure your real estate business to take advantage of 1031 exchanges — even if your process starts with a renovation. The key is to think like an investor from day one, not a dealer. Your intent, your documentation, and your holding period all matter enormously. When in doubt, work with a qualified real estate CPA who understands the nuances of dealer vs. investor classification.
